summary: Specifies extensions to the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol so that a stateful PCE can compute and initiate Segment Routing traffic-engineering paths, and so a client can ask for a path with constraints and optimization criteria.

eli5.summary: A map service can figure out the route and tell the traveler which turns to follow. This teaches that service how to give turn lists for segment routing.

questions: what is maximum sid depth in pcep
subtitle: How a path computation server hands Segment Routing label lists to routers, and how routers say what they can handle.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing lets a head-end router steer packets along an ordered list of segments, but PCEP had no way to carry such a list or to say which routers can use one.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8664 adds a new path setup type (PST 1), a capability sub-TLV that advertises the maximum SID depth, and an SR-ERO subobject (type 36) that carries a SID, a node or adjacency identifier, or both.
tldr.outcome: A stateful PCE can compute and initiate SR-TE paths on a PCC, and a PCC can request one. The RFC updates RFC 8408 and has itself been updated by RFC 9756 and RFC 9933.

today: RFC 8664 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 8408 and has itself been updated by RFC 9756 and RFC 9933, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: Why PCEP Needs Segment Routing Extensions
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) is a source-routing approach. The ingress node steers a packet along a path given as an ordered list of instructions called segments, without hop-by-hop signaling such as LDP or RSVP-TE. This document is relevant to the MPLS forwarding plane only, where an SR path corresponds to an MPLS Label Switching Path.

The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) already lets a Path Computation Client (PCC) talk to a Path Computation Element (PCE), and its stateful and PCE-initiated extensions let a PCE compute and set up LSPs. RFC 8664 adds what is missing so that a stateful PCE can compute and initiate SR-TE paths, and so that a PCC can request an SR path from a stateful or stateless PCE.

It relies on RFC 8408 for exchanging the SR capability and for naming Segment Routing as the path setup type, and it updates that RFC to clarify the use of sub-TLVs in the PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV. It is also meant as a way for a network controller (the PCE) to install candidate paths of an SR Policy on a head-end node (the PCC).
sections.eli5: Routers that use segment routing follow a list of stops written on the packet. A helper computer can work out the best list, and this document is the language it uses to hand the list to the router.

sections.title: How PCEP Works in an SR Network
sections.content:
In an SR network the ingress node prepends a header made of a list of SIDs (MPLS labels, in this document) to every outgoing packet. With the information the IGP distributes, that list is enough to guide the packet to the egress node, so no signaling protocol is needed.

PCEP carries path information in the Explicit Route Object (ERO), a sequence of subobjects. This RFC defines a new SR-ERO subobject that can carry a SID and the identity of the node or adjacency the SID stands for. An ERO with SR-ERO subobjects can appear in a PCRep, a PCInitiate, a PCUpd and a PCRpt message. A PCC can also report the path it actually uses in a Record Route Object (RRO), for which the RFC defines a matching SR-RRO subobject.

The same machinery supports migration. A PCE can update an LSP that was set up with RSVP-TE so that it uses an SR-TE path, and a PCC can do the same for an undelegated LSP: it requests an SR-TE path with a PCReq, establishes it in the data plane, and then tears down the original RSVP-TE path. The reverse is possible too, which the RFC describes as useful for rolling back a change.
sections.eli5: The router at the start of the trip puts a list of stops on each packet. The helper computer only has to supply the list. If the new route turns out badly, the helper can switch the traffic back to the old way.

sections.title: Advertising SR Capability and Stack Depth
sections.content:
RFC 8664 defines Path Setup Type 1: the traffic-engineering path is set up using Segment Routing. A PCEP speaker SHOULD indicate support by sending a PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV in its OPEN object with PST 1 in the list. If it lists PST 1, it MUST also include the new SR-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV (type 26, length 4). A speaker that receives this sub-TLV without PST 1 in the list MUST ignore it, and one that sees PST 1 without the sub-TLV MUST send a PCErr (Error-Type 10, Error-value 12) and close the session.

The sub-TLV has two flags and a number. The N flag says the PCC can resolve a Node or Adjacency Identifier (NAI) to a SID. The X flag says the PCC imposes no limit on the Maximum SID Depth (MSD). Otherwise the MSD field gives the maximum number of SIDs the PCC can push onto a packet, and it MUST be greater than zero. If both X and MSD are zero, the PCE MUST send a PCErr (Error-value 21) and close the session.

With a non-zero MSD on a session, the PCE MUST NOT send SR-TE paths with more SIDs than that. A PCC that needs a different MSD MUST close the session and re-establish it. If the session's MSD is zero, the PCC MAY give a limit per request using the new METRIC object type 11 (maximum SID depth). A PCE may learn a per-node or per-interface MSD from routing protocols instead, and in that case the routing value takes precedence over the one in the sub-TLV.
sections.eli5: Before they start working together, the router tells the helper two things: whether it can look up a stop by name, and how many stops it can write on one packet. The helper must keep its lists within that limit.

sections.title: The SR-ERO Subobject
sections.content:
An ERO that carries an SR-TE path MUST contain only SR-ERO subobjects, and each one MUST carry at least a SID or an NAI. The PCC builds its MPLS label stack as a last-in-first-out stack: the first subobject gives the topmost label and the last gives the bottommost.

The subobject starts with the L flag (loose hop), then Type 36, a Length (at least 8 and a multiple of 4), the 4-bit NT field that says what kind of NAI follows, and flag bits F, S, C and M. A 4-octet SID and a variable NAI follow, each optional.

  • M set: the SID is an MPLS label stack entry; otherwise it is an index into the SRGB or SRLB.
  • C set (with M): the PCE specifies the TC, S and TTL fields, though the PCC MAY override them.
  • S set: the SID is absent and the PCC chooses it, for example by looking up the NAI in the SR database. M and C MUST then be zero.
  • F set: the NAI is absent. F MUST be set exactly when NT is 0.

NT values 0 to 6 cover an absent NAI, IPv4 and IPv6 node IDs, an IPv4 adjacency, an IPv6 adjacency with global addresses, an unnumbered adjacency with IPv4 node IDs, and an IPv6 adjacency with link-local addresses. The SR-RRO subobject has the same format without the L flag, and its first subobject identifies the first segment the LSP visits.
sections.eli5: Each stop on the list is a small card. The card says which stop it is, either by its number, by its name, or both. A few tick boxes on the card tell the router how to read it.

sections.title: Validating and Applying the SR-ERO
sections.content:
When a PCC receives an SR-ERO it first checks that the Length, S bit, F bit and NT field agree. For example, with NT=1 (IPv4 node ID) the F bit MUST be zero and the Length MUST be 8 if S is 1, otherwise 12. A mismatch makes the whole ERO invalid and the PCC MUST send a PCErr with Error-Type 10 and Error-value 11 (malformed object). Other checks reject an ERO that mixes SR-ERO with other subobject types, mixes SIDs of different kinds (label, index, none), or carries label value 3 (Implicit NULL), which the PCC MUST NOT accept. An Adj-SID subobject MUST NOT have the L flag set.

To act on a valid ERO the PCC converts it into an MPLS label stack plus a next hop, then prepends the stack to packets and sends them to that next hop. Index values are turned into labels using the procedure in RFC 8660. If only NAIs are given, the PCC first looks for a matching prefix or adjacency that has a SID. If it cannot resolve a SID or a router's SRGB or SRLB, or an index is too big for the block, it MUST send a PCErr with Error-Type 10 and a specific error value (14 to 19). Too many labels for the PCC gives Error-value 3.

If an ERO would change the path of an existing LSP and any of these errors occurs, the PCC MUST NOT update the LSP. RRO processing follows the same syntax rules, with matching errors for an empty or mixed RRO.
sections.eli5: The router reads each card and checks it makes sense: the right size, no mixed-up kinds, and every name it can find on its map. If anything is off, it tells the helper and keeps using the old route.

sections.title: Operating and Migrating a Network
sections.content:
Segment Routing is one path setup type among others, so it can run alongside RSVP-TE or alone. Both the PCC and PCE must list PST 1 and include the SR-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV before it can be used. A PCE that initiates an LSP proposes the type in the PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV of the SRP object, and the PCC MAY accept it or reject the request. A PCC that requests a path can name a preferred type in the RP object, and the PCE MAY reply with a different type or reject the request.

Implementations MUST let the operator enable and disable the SR path setup type, and PCE and PCC implementations MUST let the operator specify SR or RSVP-TE as the proposed or nominated type.

The migration steps are to enable the SR PST on the PCEs, enable it on the PCCs, and reset each PCEP session. If there is a problem the operator can disable the SR PST and reset the sessions to roll back. A session reset does not disturb the data plane: LSPs that were already set up stay in place. Enabling the SR PST does not move user traffic onto SR LSPs by itself, which is out of scope. Implementations SHOULD log capability mismatches and cases where a different PST was used than proposed, with the reason.
sections.eli5: Switching to the new way is like flipping a switch on the helper and on each router, then restarting their chat. If something goes wrong, flip the switches back. Cars already on the road keep driving the whole time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5440, RFC 8231, RFC 8281 and RFC 8408 apply, and the RFC states that no additional security measures are required. It does add two cautions.

First, this specification lets a controller instantiate a path without a hop-by-hop signaling protocol such as RSVP-TE. If the PCEP session has no integrity protection, an attacker could create a path that is not subjected to the verification checks a signaling protocol would perform.

Second, the MSD field in the Open message discloses how many MPLS labels the sender can push. Without strong encryption on the session, an attacker could use it to learn about the capabilities of edge devices in the network.
sections.eli5: If a stranger could talk to the router in this language, they could give it a route nobody double-checked. They could also learn how long a list the router can handle. So the chat needs to be protected.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: Loose hop flag; if zero the PCC must not overwrite the SID.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length in octets; at least 8 and a multiple of 4.

fields.name: NT
fields.desc: Type of the NAI that follows, if any.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Other bits must be zero and are ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: TC, S and TTL specified by the PCE.

fields.name: M
fields.desc: SID is an MPLS label stack entry.

fields.name: SID (optional)
fields.desc: Index into the SRGB or SRLB, or an MPLS label stack entry.

items.label: IPv4 adjacency
items.desc: A pair of IPv4 addresses, 8 octets.

items.label: IPv6 global adjacency
items.desc: A pair of global IPv6 addresses, 32 octets.

items.label: Unnumbered adjacency
items.desc: Node ID and interface ID pairs with IPv4 node IDs, 16 octets.

items.label: IPv6 link-local adjacency
items.desc: Global IPv6 address and interface ID pairs, 40 octets.
